facts.statement: Born Hastings, England, 1888; emigrated to Canada 1906; died 1938.
Trapper and writer; Anahareo encouraged his change towards beaver conservation.
Presented himself as Grey Owl while concealing his English origins.
Men of the Last Frontier published 1931; naturalist working with the national parks.

interpretation.note: Interpretation of the documented life and works; no claim of personal acquaintance from shared themes.

appraisal.note: AETERNUS editorial judgement; not presented as a historical quotation.

en.tagline: A borrowed identity, and a real argument for the living forest.
en.intro: Grey Owl’s public life rested on a concealed origin. Born Archibald Belaney in England, he became a celebrated spokesman for the Canadian wilderness under an assumed indigenous identity. The deception and the conservation work both belong to his history.
en.orientation: Anahareo’s place in that history is essential. Her influence helped turn a trapper towards the protection of beavers and the writing that made him widely known.
origin: Belaney left Hastings for Canada in 1906. Life in northern Ontario brought trapping, guiding and close contact with people whose knowledge helped him inhabit the country.
career: The national parks gave his work a new setting in 1931. Public speaking and books carried a conservation message beyond the cabin and the lake, while the Grey Owl persona obscured the author’s actual background.
literature: Men of the Last Frontier combines knowledge of woodland life with a plea for its preservation. It is written at the crossing of an older trapping world and a growing public concern for wildlife.
en.legacy: The force of the writing survives within a damaged claim to authority. Reading it with Anahareo’s contribution and Belaney’s origins in view restores the complexity of its making.
en.bridge: The book belongs to the history of conservation and to the history of the persona through which that cause was presented.
